items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0028, relevance_score=0.308] The Present Studies and Hypotheses

The current research explores the idea of mental representation with the aim of understanding why individuals have such difficulty categorizing multiracial faces as such. Rather than employ a categorization task, however, we ask (a) how multiracial faces are psychologically organized in perceivers' minds and (b) whether this organization might explain the low rates of categorizing multiracial faces as multiracial observed in the explicit categorization data.

[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.241] Based on evidence of hypodescent, we reason that multiracial faces could be mentally represented along with socially subordinated monoracial faces (i.e., groups that have been judged as less dominant by the broader culture), perhaps being confused with those monoracial faces that are especially low in racial prototypicality. The latter prediction derives from research indicating that low prototypicality and multiracialism have been operationalized using the exact same procedures (e.g., Brooks & Gwinn, 2010; Ma, Kantner, et al., 2021).

[PAPER_0102, relevance_score=0.242] The faces that we used in the present studies were categorized as Latinx in the norming data more than as any other categories that were provided in the response set to norming participants (i.e., Asian, Black, Hispanic/Latina/o, White, or Other). We also wish to note that in the preregistration, we use the gendered label Latina/o to describe the category we refer to as Latinx in the current article. This decision to switch to using Latinx was intentionally made to promote inclusivity for individuals who identify outside of a binary conception of gender.
items.paper_content_summary: The paper describes a hypothesis that multiracial faces are distinct from high- but not low-prototypicality Asian, White, and Latinx faces. It also considers possible perceptual confusion with socially subordinated monoracial or Latinx faces and asks whether perceptual organization explains categorization [PAPER_0057] [PAPER_0037] [PAPER_0038] [PAPER_0028].

[PAPER_0041, relevance_score=0.358] Study 1

Method

Participants

The targeted sample size was determined based on the number of face stimuli included in the study. The literature lacks definitive guidelines for determining sample sizes in MDS (Rodgers, 1991), but Monte Carlo simulations have suggested 20 ratings be obtained for each pairwise judgment (Davison, 1983). We aimed to have each face pair rated an average of 50 times total, but due to a calculation error, both left/right orderings of each face pair were rated an average of 50 times, inadvertently doubling the ratings per pair.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.304] Each pair was rated an average of 97.95 times (SD = 10.14; min = 63). Participants were 1,285 Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) workers. items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.285] Results and Discussion

We aggregated similarity judgments across participants and computed an average judgment for each face pair to create a similarity matrix.3 The matrix was submitted to MDS procedures using the PROXSCAL function in SPSS. Following previous literature on the MDS of faces, we assumed a Euclidean distance metric (e.g., Busey, 1998; Byatt & Rhodes, 2004; Knapp et al., 2006; Valentine, 1991). An eight-dimension solution had an s-stress value of 0.0351.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.331] An examination of the Dispersion Accounted For statistic, a measure characterizing the variance explained by the MDS solution, revealed that this eight-dimension solution explained 98.93% of the variance in the similarity judgments.

Planned correlational analysis was conducted to identify the latent factors underlying each dimension. We correlated each dimension with perceived demographic data, subjective ratings data, and objective facial features taken from the CFD (Tables 1-3).

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.361] Studies 1-3 were preregistered. We deviated from the preregistered analysis plan in the following ways. First, rather than visually inspecting the perceptual maps and using analysis of variance to test whether the faces were categorically bound, we used DFA to classify the faces. This strategy offers a more definitive and appropriate test of the hypotheses. Second, guided by recent findings in the face perception literature (reviewed in the introduction), we adopted an eight-dimension solution for the MDS data rather than determining the dimension structure for each study individually.

It used category-level and prototypicality-level discriminant function analyses (DFAs) and also conducted MDS on standardized scores. The paper discloses changes to the preregistered analysis plan. First, rather than visually inspecting the perceptual maps and using analysis of variance to test whether the faces were categorically bound, we used DFA to classify the faces.
